utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in the courtroom, this is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MFIs still pending from yesterday, I take it that you will receive shortly by e-mail, please prepare for your position in respect of those exhibits which are still MFIed, and then we'll deal with them later this morning. Mr. Waespi, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Yes, my colleague, Prashanthi Mahindaratne will lead this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne. Has the Chamber no protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then that would be Mr. Flynn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Mr. Edward Flynn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Perhaps I could already explore whether we need to spend much time on admission of the 92 ter statement. Does the Chamber hear any objections? I see Mr. Cayley nodding no; Mr. Kurzmanovic nodding no; Mr. Misetic nodding no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Flynn, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by the usher. I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Flynn. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne who is counsel for the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you indicated that we do not need to spend too much time in admitting the 92 ter submission. Am I still required to go through the preliminary questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, of course, I was just wondering whether, as to the content, whether we would expect any objections by the Defence. But, of course, for admission, Rule 92 ter says exactly what the witness has to ascertain before a statement can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Edward J. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you interviewed by investigators attached to the Office of the Prosecutor in June 1997, 29th June 1997?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That interview, do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you provided with a transcript of that interview subsequently?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did it reflect accurately the statements you made to the investigators on 29th June 1997?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you sign that transcript and provide it to the Office of the Prosecutor as your statement in relation to the subject matter of this case on 3rd May 1998?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On 26th and 27th of February, 2008, did you provide a further supplementary statement to the Office of the Prosecutor including clarifications to your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 4781 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, last Sunday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar that needs a number to be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, last Sunday, 6th April, did you examine your statement of 3rd May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked today in court the same questions asked of you by the investigators in June 1997, subject to the clarifications you provided in your supplementary statement of 2008, would your answers be the same as those reflected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are the contents of your statement of 3rd May 1998 true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That statement of Mr. Flynn given 26th and 27th of February, 2008, is that a separate document that it needs to be a number to be assigned, or is it an annex to the other statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. They are separate statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the 2008 statement, I think, Mr. Registrar, needs, if he hasn't got it already, a number so that it can be put on our screens and that an exhibit number can be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's document number 4782, if that can be called up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become P21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P21. It's still not on our screen, but I take it that we'll see it appear soon. No objections, as far as I understand, to both statements. In the absence of any objections, P20 and P21 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, when you made your supplementary statement on 26th and 27th February, 2008, did you examine a number of documents?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were they all or were most of Human Rights Action Team reports authored or co-authored by you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you identify those documents and authenticate them by way of your supplementary statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Last Sunday, 6th April, did you examine those documents?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied or were you satisfied that the contents of those documents were true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has authenticated 25 documents and two videos by way of the supplementary statement P21, which were also submitted as part of the 92 ter submission. Could those documents be given sequential P numbering and admitted into evidence at this stage, or am I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked the witness about documents, not about videos, but I take it that you have reviewed those videos as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And are you the author of the videos or were you involved in production?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in the production, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you, then -- I mean what did you authenticate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present when they were filmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were present when they were filmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I would be playing clips, segments of those two videos in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But since you asked the witness only about the documents, I wondered about the videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. I suggest that the registrar prepares a list, that this list will be distributed so that we all know what we are talking about, 25 documents, that he will provisionally assigned P numbers to them, and that we will then hear whether there's any objection, and then a decision can be taken on admission. Meanwhile, you are invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Would this be the appropriate stage, Mr. President, to read out the summary of the witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you kept it short. It's to inform the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Edward Flynn is a senior human rights officer attached to the United Nations Counter-Terrorism Committee. In August 1994, he took up appointment as a human rights field officer and the coordinator of the Zagreb field office of the United Nations High Commissioner For Human Rights. On 7th August, 1995, Mr. Flynn arrived in Knin to take up leadership and organise a system referred to as Human Rights Action Teams. Human Rights Action Teams was set up in response to the human rights violations committed in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm. The teams comprised of monitors from several UN agencies present on the ground who patrolled the territory together as well as separately and reported the information collectively. Mr. Flynn functioned as a member of the Human Rights Action Teams from 7th August to 17th September; and in this capacity, patrolled the southern part of the Krajina. He witnessed instances of looting by members of the HV and burning and destruction of property in the immediate presence of soldiers. He observed and reported extensive destruction of hamlets villages, and towns, and the recovery of a number of bodies of killed civilians. He reported on complaints received of harassment and intimidation of the remaining Serb population at the hands of members of the Croatian forces. Mr. Flynn was one of the first international monitors to be present in Grubori on 25th August, 1995, and witnessed the burning houses and barns and the bodies of the civilians executed in the incident. Mr. Flynn participated in a number of meetings with the accused Ivan Cermak when the crimes were discussed. He describes Cermak's reactions to that information. Mr. President, that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I proceed, may I be permitted to provide the witness with a binder containing hard copies of the documents as well as hard copies of the statements? The reason being is there are a number of documents involved; and in the course of his testimony, the witness would be required to cross refer between the documents and the statements. And while, of course, we would rely on the -- on e-court for the document being discussed in court principally, I believe that the system would make it more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sounds very practical. No objections? Please proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have provided the binder to Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, in that binder, you have hard copies of your statement that clipped on, both statements as well as the documents, arranged chronologically in tab 4, if you are required to look at them.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 2068 to be brought on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is not among the 25 you referred to earlier, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will get a number. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since it has not got a number so far, Mr. President, I will use the 65 ter numbers in my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you happen to have assigned a number already to this one, because we have no access to 65 ter numbers, the Chamber has access to P numbers only. No, that's not correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if I could refer you to your 2008 statement and I'm referring to P21, at paragraph 11, you refer to your observations made on a patrol taken in the Krajina on 13th August, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the document that was just called up on the screen, if you could focus on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You recalled your observations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you recalled that the human rights action team travelled to Benkovac through Kistanje and Djeverske on Sunday, and you go on to say: "It is a fair assessment to say that the Krajina is burning. Dozens of fire locations were observed and the view over the Benkovac valley showed at least ten huge plumes of smoke in different locations. Houses were still being set ablaze in Kistanje and the surrounding area and whole folds were burning everywhere. Kistanje, Djeverske, Otric, and other towns have become virtually unlivable by actions which occurred after the fighting. The authorities continue to take no action. The human rights action team believes this issue must be raised at the highest levels for one reason, because it," you then go on to report your observations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is that your own report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that based on your personal observations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that, in a supplementary statement of 2008, P21, at paragraph 11, you state as follows: "It was on this day that we truly became alarmed at the growing scale of destruction, as it began to look like auto systematic campaign." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that statement? What were the factors that led you and your fellow -- your colleagues to suspect a systematic campaign behind the destruction?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, it was the scale of the burning, the number of houses and fields that were burning, the geographic range of the burning, because a couple of days earlier, we had seen a large number of fires on the road between Knin and Drnis. There were also a number of reports at that time from some other UN observers in the field, and we also noted that virtually all this burning was taking place in areas in which all combat activities had stopped. So there seemed to be no plausible connection, if anyone wished to make one, between any ongoing fighting and the burning. These were areas that seemed to have -- in which the fighting had stopped. It was approximately a week since the end of active military activities in the major villages and towns, and yet there were a very large number of fires taking place. So, I would also add that there had been sporadic reports at that point about uniformed individuals with equipment that might be used to set fires, and so we took that into account as well. But, principally, it was the extremely large scale and simply large number of fires.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, in your 2008 statement, that is P21, in paragraph 12, you referred to the presence of a UN TV crew on that particular patrol, and I'm referring to the 13th August patrol, which recorded footage of the destruction you observed. Is that correct? I'm referring you to paragraph 11 of your -- I'm sorry, paragraph 12 of your 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen that footage since?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Since that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since that day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is one of the videotapes that were submitted with the 92 ter submission, and that entire video contains 12 minutes and 48 seconds of footage; however, to save court time, we have selected five short clips which runs two, three minutes and 58 seconds which we will show in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of it is tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The entire tape is tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections to playing only part of it? I take it the Defence teams have had an opportunity to view. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could, we will play that on sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, since there is no narration in the course of running the tape, I will ask a few questions relating to the footage, if that is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Always referring to the time when it stops. So if the question is about a certain picture, please indicate where the timer is on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, I'm not referring to a particular segment of this tape, but can you tell if, in fact, this footage is being filmed from the vehicle that you were in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. This was being filmed from a second vehicle. We were two vehicles driving from Knin through Kistanje and Djeverske to Benkovac that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to identify, generally, this area in which you are patrolling through?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is Kistanje. It may be just going into Djeverske, but I'm pretty sure it's Kistanje. You can see the smoke in the background.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the document I just read, the paragraph, there was a reference to plumes of smoke in the Benkovac valley. Can you identify this area that is being shown right now, and that's about four seconds and -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make it minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Minutes, I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Those were the plumes of smoke we saw in the Benkovac value at different locations. You can see it also in this picture here with our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the area from which these plumes of smoke are rising?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That's generally to the west. It's in the direction of Djeverske and Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you go a little bit further and pause by that road sign. Can you pause there, please. Mr. President, we have a clearer picture of that still. If we could call up 4809, that is a still of that last frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to tender this as a separate document or is it just to assist us in better viewing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Trial Chamber, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, could you just please read that sign board for the record and the directions indicated on that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, it says: Kistanje is straight ahead, Bilanovici is to the left, and Knin is to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that plume of smoke you could see in the background, from where is it rising?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: The direction of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where were the vehicles going at this stage, towards which direction?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: We were going toward Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, if we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you generally identify this area, and there I'm referring to 6 minutes and 32 seconds on the time slot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. These are images of burning buildings in Kistanje along the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We could move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask, if you have just one moment. You said, "burning buildings." It looks to me very much as a burnt buildings. I don't see any fire at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Your Honour. This building we're looking at right now is not burning, as far as I can see. I recall this video. I think we'll see burning in a moment. So I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We consider it significant, if I may say, that there seem to be no destruction as from some sort of weapon fire on the sides of these buildings. There's evident smoke, indications on the side of the building, and the roof has caved in. So, this building that we're looking at now was not actually burning, but it looked to me as if it had been destroyed by fire, rather than by some sort of weapons fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to ask that, if a shell falls on the roof and causes a fire, would you see any different if the roof than further burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly not, but I would expect there might be some more damage to the walls, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say, due to the explosion, you would see some traces on the walls as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did see, during the course of my time in the conflict area, not only during these two weeks, a large number of buildings that had been destroyed by military activity, by weapons fire, and walls were shattered and there were mortar holes in the walls and that sort of thing. I don't see very much evidence of that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, that discussion was when the tape was paused at 6 minutes and 57 seconds. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's me getting out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we just pause there for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, can you identify the person who is recorded taking a photograph here in this frame?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. That's Alun Robert who was the chief information officer for the UN mission that was based in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is at 7 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, the sign boards indicate Zadar, 72, Benkovac, and Ervenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, to ask you a question there, the sign board for Ervenik, does that have an arrow head. Can you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It looks to me like there might have been an arrow head on the right-hand side. It looks like it might have broken off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you identify this area? I ask that because since there is no arrow head on the board Ervenik, it seems as if it's -- it announces the name of the place. What is this area which is being filmed here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I think it is the centre of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We could move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an act of fire here. Again, there are buildings that seemed to have collapsed roofs, but relatively little damage, I would say, to the sides, to the walls. You can see the fire inside the building here, and the roof has collapsed at least in part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's at minutes 8 and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Flynn, you said that you saw buildings on fire in response to a question from the Judge. Did you see many buildings on fire, ablaze?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That day, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you present during the whole time the footage, the 12 minutes and 58 seconds of footage were recorded on this particular patrol?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's 12 minutes and 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. We could move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The roof is collapsing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you would allow me one additional question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked about possibility of a shell falling, hitting a roof. Were any combat activities reported, let's say, in the 48 hours preceding the moment you visited the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe there was, Your Honour. I was aware of the reports that had come into the UN headquarters in Knin, and your reference would be to the 11th of August and I don't recall that there was any combat activity in that particular area on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not any shelling, not any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the Kistanje area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call for document number 2131 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, in your 1998 statement, and that is P20, from page 25 on to page 30, you have described what you observed in the hamlet of Grubori on 25th August, 1995. I'm referring to your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 25 going on to page 30.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It relates to your observations in Grubori on 25th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you observe the screen, the Human Rights Action Team report, for the period 24th to 27th August, includes the observations made by Human Rights Action Teams in Grubori on 25th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, actually just one team on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that a team in which you were included?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus on paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a detailed report of what you observed in Grubori. Is that your own report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that an accurate report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, according to this report, and what you have stated in your own 1998 statement, the Human Rights Action Teams observed five bodies of the civilians killed in the Grubori incident on 25th; and further down the report, there is a reference to all the bodies or a number of five bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. We did not see all five of those bodies, though, on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There was three -- can you explain as to how the bodies were observed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: On the 25th, we just saw two of those deceased individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: My colleague saw three others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, of the five bodies, you observed two; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you have given a detailed description of the observations of yourself and the other members of the Human Rights Action Team in your statement of 1998 from page 25 to 30?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of 2008, that is P21, at paragraph 25, you refer to a UN TV crew being present in Grubori with your patrol and filming the scene in Grubori in your presence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen that footage since?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this tape that is 2576 also has been tendered under the 92 ter submission. However, this tape is a compilation of footage by UN TV which contains, in addition to the footage relate to go Grubori, the footage of destruction which was just submitted, just played in court. Therefore, the Prosecution does not tender the entire tape in evidence, only the segment which will be played in court now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in order to avoid whatever confusion, is there a possibility that you prepare a new version on which only the portion played is visible and that we assign a separate exhibit number to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That, then, will have a -- precisely what we see and how long that footage is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think it can be played on sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand the whole of the entire tape is tendered in evidence; so, therefore, it would certainly be -- if we make it clear what we see at this moment so that we know what is tendered and what is actually played, I think that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, of this tape, from 42 seconds to 3 minutes and 20 seconds will be presented in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- which is 2 minutes and 51 seconds of footage. That is the only footage we are relying on at this stage, since part of the footage has already been tendered in evidence. The tape also includes a couple of excerpts of an interview with the accused Ivan Cermak, which the Prosecution will tender in evidence later on through the correct, appropriate channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm a bit confused, Ms. Mahindaratne. You say that's all on the tape in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The tape is a compilation of footage which has footage of Grubori, the footage of destruction in Kistanje which we just observed, as well as two excerpts of an interview with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you tendered the whole of that compilation tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have submitted the entire tape under the 92 ter submission, Mr. President, but I will only submit the footage which will be presented in court in evidence at this stage. So, as you directed, we will present a further tape with only this clip to prevent any further confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not entirely clear. The whole of the tape, you say, is attached to the 92 ter statement. It is an attachment to the 92 ter statement. You're seeking the 92 ter statement to be admitted including attachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the whole of at that tape, you're seeking to be admitted into evidence. And if you now say we rely only on a portion of it, I do understand that at this moment, in relation to this witness, you rely only on this portion of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you're seeking the whole of the tape to be admitted into evidence, then, of course, the Prosecution relies on this tape in its entirety as well otherwise. But I take it that at later stages, you will refer to other portions and put questions to witnesses in relation to other portions of that video. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There was a mistake in submitting the entire tape with the 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then, what you are telling me now is that part of that compilation should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And only this portion, I do understand, remains as an attachment to the 92 ter statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Otherwise, there would be duplicity since we have already tendered the footage of destruction in Kistanje under a separate 65 ter number and also the interview with the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you withdraw the compilation video in it's entirety, and it's replaced by separate portions. We've seen one of Kistanje and we'll now see one of Grubori. That's the only thing and the remainder is out. We don't have to bother about the video in it's entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is only with regard to this video, and not the previous video that I referred to. The previous video of Kistanje -- there are two videos tendered with the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we had two videos. One was already limited to Kistanje. That doesn't change in any way. Now, what we are seeing now was part of a compilation; but as the remainder, anything else apart from the portion we'll see now, you'll remove that and what remains is the Grubori video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. I'm sorry for that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, better avoided.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we have the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "We visited the Plavno Valley yesterday, to meet with a group of residents in one town there. We observed that across the valley another town was apparently on fire. There was a huge plume of smoke and so we visited that town in the afternoon, and we found that, in fact, almost every structure in this hillside village was in flames." "The villagers said they had been called away to a meeting in a nearby village. That meeting never took place."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We waited at the school and no one came. When we looked up here, we saw that everything was on fire. We rushed back. There is no one here now. There is no sign of those who stayed behind. Whether they burned or ran away, we don't know." "My husband is missing. He may have been burned. Granny is missing. She may have been burned. She is very old and couldn't run away." "When the fire finally died down, Dusanka and her neighbour were able to search the houses and were able to search the houses. Later, she showed the UN human rights team where they have found their husbands."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Here, let me show you. That one was not here. Her husband was ill. He was lying in bed over there. When we came, we found him dead. That's all I can tell you." "He couldn't hear. He was deaf." "Look, you see, he's been shot. Shot in the head." "They were wailing and grief stricken because in the interim they found two dead bodies, people who had been killed evidently earlier that day. One person had been shot through the head. Another person, both of them were elderly men, had his throat slashed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We were looking for our husbands everywhere. I found my husband near the cows. The cows were dead, and granny was not there. She was burned in the house. She was ill and she was burned in her bed. This one here, she wasn't here either. When she came, she found her husband dead in the house." "These Croatian police vehicles were parked one kilometre away, and a local military governor admitted police troops had carried out the military operation in the same village of Grubor."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, was that an accurate record of what you observed in Grubori on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, right at the end, there were a line of vehicles parked. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your statement of 1998, and I'm referring to P20, that is your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At page 28, in line -- lines 2 to 8, you referred to -- you referred to "noticing a long line of parked police vehicles unattended which was parked along the side of the road, and we drove past the police vehicles." Do you, in fact, recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now were those vehicles that we saw in the footage here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you refer to police vehicles. How did you figure out, how did you conclude that they were police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, they weren't standard military vehicles. They weren't green coloured armoured cars or jeeps. They were almost all of the same type of vehicle, either blue or white. There might have been a grey one or two. So they were clearly government vehicles. They weren't civilian vehicles, and there wasn't a marking on them. But it was really by process of elimination, if you will, that we concluded, and I concluded, that they were police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you state in -- in your 1998 statement in those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Mahindaratne. The witness tells us that "by elimination," what did you eliminate exactly which led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, they were not military vehicles. They did not seem to be connected to any sort of military operation, at least by their appearance. They were not civilian vehicles, as I say. They were not -- I mean, they were not privately-owned vehicles. Those would have been readily identifiable, a lot older, and of different makes. These were vehicles that, as I say, were practically uniform in their appearance, apart from the colour varying between blue and white. But they were unmarked vehicles, at least with respect to the side of the vehicles, as I recall, and I don't think that the licence plates either gave an indication that they were police vehicles. So there was no explicit indication that they were police vehicles, but that was a conclusion that we made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just add one more thing, Your Honour, please. Just that it was also striking that these vehicles were parked really in the middle of nowhere. They were along the side of the road. There was no residence nearby. There was no building. There was no office. There was just empty land. So we assumed that there must have been some connection to some sort of security force or other, and likely police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It still puzzles me a bit, but, of course, I do understand that you would not expect them to be of a hunting party or something like that at that moment. But, of course, there are a lot of explanations possible. If you see a lot of vehicles in the middle of nowhere, you also could say that it is an indication that there are not police vehicles because you would expect police vehicles near to a police office. It's just the way you reason, you're reasoning. I'm trying to test a bit of your -- on what exactly your conclusion is based. You say they were not privately owned, but you also told us that from the licence plates, you couldn't see that they were police vehicles. You could also, when reasoning, you could say, since the licence plates did not give any indication they were police vehicles, my conclusion is that they were privately owned. I mean I'm just trying to find out exactly what the basis for your conclusion is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we also were aware, and I was aware, that they weren't standard police vehicles, if you will. I mean, I was familiar with the kind of police vehicles that typically operated in other parts of Croatia at that time, which, among others things, if they were patrol vehicles would have the flashing light on the top. But these were blue and white. I mean, they clearly belonged together. I should say it may be that others in our group also suggested that they were police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As an argument for reasoning, that's not very strong, because if others were to have suggested that they were civilian vehicles, you would have accepted that as well, isn't it? I mean, you say suggestions within the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, because, as I say, I know what civilian vehicles would look like or vehicles used for agricultural activities. These were brand new, or relatively new, which was rare in that very impoverished area. As I say, they very clearly belonged together, so whoever had driven them belonged in a group; and, as I say, they weren't military vehicles of a traditional type and colour, let's say. But the vehicles did not say on the side that they were police vehicles, so there was a certain amount of deduction involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you look into the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't have a glance and note children's toys in the back seats or anything else? I'm just trying to find out how thorough your observations were which led you to believe that these were police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, throughout that operation, Your Honour, we were fairly cautious about the extent to which we examined some matters up close. I mean for example, we rarely interviewed Croatian military personnel we saw, because it was a highly-charged situation and it was still -- there was still an element of risk involved. We didn't stop and look into the vehicles, I think just because we felt that it was wiser to observe them, to film them, and to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps, Ms. Mahindaratne, at the very end, we could have a look at these vehicles on the video, not necessarily immediately now, but just to digest the information we just received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, on that point, could you describe the Grubori area? Where was the hamlet of Grubori located in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It is in an area called the Plavno Valley which is accessible mainly by a single road branching off the main road going north out of Knin. It's fairly remote. The villages are very small. They are more appropriately called hamlets, I would say. It's an agricultural area. There is not a lot of development. I mean, there's -- most of the area is open, and I think it was used for agricultural purposes. But generally it's quite remote.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what type of a road was that through which you had to access Grubori? Was it a sort of a main roadway where you might see generally a few vehicles travelling through during the day, or is it a small, remote route?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. It was a very simple bumpy dirt road, very small. I think two vehicles would have difficulty passing on that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, generally, would you expect to see traffic on that road?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Maybe a handful of vehicles. Probably many days go by when there is no traffic or there was no traffic on that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do the residents in the Plavno Valley generally go about by vehicles or what? Can you give some sense to the Trial Chamber as to what you meant by "remote"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I doubt they had vehicles, for the most part, apart from agricultural vehicles, but I'm really not too sure about that. But this was a very simple hamlet, and it was really just a very small farming community.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on page 28 of your 1998 statement, P20, your previous statement, page 28 from lines 2 to 8, you also mention that you took down the -- you noted the licence plate numbers of those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you do with that information? Did you submit it to the Croatian authorities, the Croatian police, or did you send it to an international entity?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. We kept that in our file, and I forwarded that information to our headquarters in Zagreb. So it was -- I mean, it came into the possession of my main office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware that that information has been taken to a logical conclusion in terms of identification of those licence plate numbers as belonging to particular vehicles? Are you aware that that has happened?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I believe the information was then, regarding the licence plate numbers, was taken by the Special Rapporteur of the UN commission on human rights, Mrs. Elisabeth Rehn; and I believe it was then forwarded to the Croatian authorities with a request for further information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, do we know anything about the information received or will that come at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that evidence will be led later on. The licence plates have been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Flynn, you took photographs in Grubori of the deceased person you saw initially, and you stated so in your statement, and the burning structures.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for photograph 4790, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you generally travel about with a camera, or did you happen to have a camera on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I didn't usually travel with a camera during those weeks, but I did happen to have a camera that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was there someone on your patrol who generally carried a camera around?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Alun Roberts often had a camera. He had a UN issued camera in connection with his information duties, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, can you please identify the photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: This is the man who had been shot and whose body we saw on the late afternoon of the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where was this body?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It was in his bedroom on the second floor of a house in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note a bullet casing on his lap?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. There is one bullet casing there, and we saw one more bullet casing on the floor that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, in total, how many bullet casings did you see in the bedroom of this deceased person?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you take photographs of the burning structures in Grubori -- I'm sorry. You just said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May have document -- photograph 4783, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say as to approximately how many structures were on fire in Grubori when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That would be a little difficult at this point, but I would estimate about ten or 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you identify the document -- the photograph on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yeah, this is one of the burning buildings in Grubori that we saw that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we bring up photograph number 4784, please. Mr. President, may I just submit all these photographs together, or would you prefer if I admitted them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne. Are these part of the 25 documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then they're not. Then, yes, I'm a bit confused. Whenever you introduce any document which is not covered by your list of 25, you should indicate, so that we can ask Mr. Registrar to assign a number to it. I think it could be a series of photographs. How many are there in total?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There are altogether seven photographs, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven photographs. I think we can have them under one number. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be number P22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President, eight photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Eight photographs which are P22. Mr. Registrar has although received the 65 ter numbers of them? I suggest to the parties, and also to you, that if you come with a larger number of exhibits, that you have them all listed. I don't know whether these are all listed in such a way that Mr. Registrar can easily assign numbers to them and easily identify which exhibit is which.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, we have notified the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from the registry if there are any problems in digesting the material presented.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The registry received a list of 29 documents to be used with this witness, but there is no indication that there are eight videos [sic] to be tendered as a single exhibit, nor is there an indication of 25 documents to be tendered as attachments to the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will all slowly learn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the videos, I take it you're referring to photos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Will you permit me to -- may I call the 65 ter numbers, so that to facilitate Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you introduce a number photograph out of these eight, please mention the 65 ter number, which will enable the registrar to get the right photos under the right number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. The first photograph which was called of the man, the body of the deceased was 65 ter number 4790. Thereafter, photograph number 4783 was called up, a burning structure. Now what we have on screen is 4784. Can we call up 4785, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, do you recognise that photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. That's another building in Grubori that was burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you take that photograph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we call up number 4786, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's another building in Grubori, and I took that photograph as well. That building is also burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up 4787, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's another photograph I took. That's a fire that we saw just as we were arriving. I was still seated in the front passenger seat of our car as we were driving into Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up 4788, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also took that photograph, and that is a haystack that was burning at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the last photograph. May I call up 4789, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I took that photograph also at the same time, and that's a photo of several pigs who had been shot -- which had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I take it that all eight photographs will go under P22?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Flynn, in your statement of 1998, if I could draw your attention to page 26, that's the first statement, lines 14 to 20, as well as if you also refer to your statement of 2008, paragraph 23, you state that you personally informed an official at Mr. Cermak's office of the Grubori incident on 25th August itself at 1630 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you described the person you conveyed this information to as Mr. Cermak's chief deputy, in your statement of 1998.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How did you know that the person was Mr. Cermak's chief deputy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: This gentleman was with General Cermak in most of the meetings with the General in which I participated. He was a person of significant rank. I think he may have been a Major. I can't recall, and I am not entirely sure of his name. But he spoke with some authority. He spoke directly to the General in the course of our meetings. He seemed to be someone in whom the General had confidence, and I assume that he was a person of significant rank, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was the information you conveyed to him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I told him of the burning that we had seen in Grubori a couple of hours previously. We actually drove directly to Knin after our first visit in the Plavno Valley because we thought it was important to notify General Cermak immediately of what we saw. We believed that the vehicles there might have had some relevance to the burning in Grubori, and we thought that this could be a good opportunity for the General and his -- those he worked with to investigate an ongoing scene, which appeared to us to be a crime scene of some kind. We had been notifying the Croatian authorities through General Cermak of a number of incidents of burning and of dead bodies we found and other things throughout the area. And in this case, we thought that, as I say, this was essentially an ongoing incident of destruction or one at least that had very recently taken place, so we thought it was important to notify General Cermak immediately. As I say, General Cermak was not available that afternoon, but his deputy was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, and I'm referring to the 1998 statement, P20, at page 28, line 29 to 32, you refer to Mr. Cermak informing the Human Rights Action Teams that the incident had occurred in the course of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did he make that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can recall the exact date. It was probably -- it was probably three or four days after the Grubori incident. That's after the 25th, so it was probably around the 28th or the 30th of August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 4029, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that among the 25?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will inform if I'm going outside the 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus on page 2, paragraph 5, which goes on to page 3 towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm referring to the registrar. If you could, if you want to, peruse the hard copies, it's at tab 1. I'm referring to the Human Rights Action Team report of 8th August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a report there of Mr. Cermak visiting the compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you present when Mr. Cermak addressed the displaced persons as reported in the Human Rights Action Team report there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is reported there that Mr. Cermak promised the displaced persons alternative accommodation if their homes were uninhabitable and also promised funds for renovation. Is that correct? Did you hear Mr. Cermak making that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I heard it through an interpreter, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you understand to be the basis for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't have -- I don't have 5 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the screen, we find B/C/S paragraph 5, but English up to and including paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 4 is the relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I mentioned paragraph 5, I mentioned it in terms of not the numerical numbers that's given because there are several paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking in terms of sequence of paragraphs on that picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. To make it clear, I'm referring to the last paragraph on page 2 going on to page 3 which refers to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was -- as you understood, what was the basis for that undertaking given by Mr. Cermak there. Why was it necessary at this stage, 8th August, 1995, for Mr. Cermak to promise the displaced persons alternative accommodation if their houses were uninhabitable or funds for renovation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, a large number of people had come to the UN compound at that point as a result of the recent fighting. Already at that point, there had been a number of structures in the area of Knin that I was aware of that were destroyed or were uninhabitable. People were fearful of leaving the compound, I think because they generally felt that their security on the outside was at risk, and some of them did not have -- they couldn't return to their homes because they had been partly or totally destroyed. So General Cermak spoke in a very assertive and authoritative manner and emphasised to the displaced persons there that they could return, and I remember the scene very well, that displaced persons were very keen to hear everything that General Cermak said because he clearly in charge. He spoke with great authority, and what I have record the in this report is the message he wished to give to the DPs, the displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph on page 3 of the same report, there is a reference to Mr. Cermak "promising to provide a list of all those killed in the fighting and burial sites, as well as a list of those now detained as prisoners of war at a local school." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To whom did he give that assurance, to the displaced persons or the UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That was also part of his statement to the displaced persons, and I wrote this report and I made an effort to include what I thought were the main points in General Cermak's statement to the displaced persons and this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we are on that document, if you could go back to page 1. In paragraph 3, I'm going by sequence there, it's reported that: "The Croatians say they have recovered, identified, and buried 61 bodies in and around Knin. Civilian/military status of the deceased is unclear." Now, in your statement of 2008, I'm referring to P21 here, at paragraph 6, you stated that you believe that that was mentioned at the same meeting where Mr. Cermak attended.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, who made that statement that 61 bodies had been we covered and that civilian/military status of the deceased is unclear? Was that Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, there is a sentence, within quotes, to the effect, "We have gone to great effort to avoid mass graves." Who said that, was it Mr. Cermak or someone else?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I believe it was General Cermak, but it may not have been. It may have been one of the other individuals with him. I'm afraid I'm really not 100 per cent sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it stated in that meeting with the displaced persons and where you attended?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. That information was communicated separately to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the statement where it says, "We have gone to great effort to avoid mass graves," within quotes, and you referred earlier to the contents of that paragraph having been said in the meeting with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not sure that information was provided to the displaced persons. I think that may have been stated to the UN in a separate meeting with General Cermak and his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you referring to a meeting conducted, held on the 8th August, the same day in the -- within the compound, or completely a separate meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. It was on the same day in the compound. General Cermak, as I recall, spoke to the displaced persons after meeting with General Forand of the UN base there and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you present at that meeting on the 8th August, 1995? You refer to it in your 2008 statement at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: You understand I have some difficulty recalling everything from those days, at least with great specificity. Yes. I was present at that meeting. I was present at quite a number of meetings with General Cermak during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 3248, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, meanwhile, I'd like to invite you to find a suitable moment within the next five minutes to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This could be a good moment, Mr. President, because I'm going on to a number of documents from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have the break right now. We'll have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before I invite you to proceed, could you tell us how much time you thought you would need, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll take about in our one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One and a half, so I think that three hours was your original --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and you're at the right speed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I expect you to finish the examination-in-chief at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, since you indicated you'd like to see the footage of the vehicles during the break, we cued it up to that point. Perhaps we could start with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This takes only a couple of seconds, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could play it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "These Croatian police vehicles were part of one ... of the military operation"

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could just pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there's at least something blue on the roof of this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Also, to point out, there is some kind of a mark, some insignia on the side of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could ask the witness why he said there was no marking on it, and what this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, do you note the marking on the side of the vehicle there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I don't know whether you recall seeing that. Do you have any recollection whatsoever now as to any aspect that led to markings on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I just didn't recall that a couple of these vehicles did have a marking on the side. So I wasn't able to tell the Court exactly how we reached the conclusion that they were police vehicles, but certainly this would be a key factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, may I move on? Do you still wish to see the footage any longer, or may I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It was just to have a renewed view on the cars. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for the document 3248 for the record. This is the Human Rights Action Team report 9th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if you refer prefer to look at the hard copy, it's at tab 2 of your binder there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus on page 2, the paragraph which is numbered 5. If you could go on to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- paragraph numbered 5. That is at the bottom of the page 2, yes. There is a reference to General Forand requesting the presence of representatives of the Centre for Human Rights and UNHCR at a meeting with Mr. Cermak. Now, were you requested by General Forand to attend this meeting on 9th August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you present at the discussion which was reported in paragraph numbered 5 going through page 3 of the document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. You mean, when the General was addressing the displaced persons? I'm sorry. The meeting immediately after --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: After with General Forand, and then going on to --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was there anything else discussed in this meeting, do you recall? If you don't recall, that is all right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yeah, I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you go on to the same document, if you move back to page 2, in paragraph 4, there is a reference that is by the paragraph numbered 4. There is a reference to "the military governor General Cermak reportedly intends to expand the scope of freedom of movement effective 10th August, possibly in the direction of Benkovac."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know, in fact, in that context whether international monitors were allowed to travel to Benkovac after this date?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, not immediately after that date. I don't think we were able to visit Benkovac until the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did it seem to you that Mr. Cermak, in fact, did have the authority to control the movement of international monitors in the area, either by relaxing restrictions or by imposing restrictions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not exactly sure of General Cermak's actual authority, but certainly he was the person we looked to, to inform us where we could and could not go. Whatever he indicated to us as areas we could visit, then we assumed that those areas could be visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were there instances when, in fact, Mr. Cermak informed the Human Rights Action Teams and the international monitors that restrictions had been relaxed and when you went, in fact, to the field, you found that those conditions were, in fact, implemented?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Almost without exception, what General Cermak told us was or was not possible in terms of movement proved to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was the mechanism that was used to restrict the movement of international monitors in the area? How was it restricted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a lot of experience with that because we did not have any wish to test the limits of our authority to travel in areas where General Cermak told us there was no freedom of movement, but there were a number of Croatian military checkpoints in the area. There was a major checkpoint at the Otric crossing which, at times, prevented us from travelling up the road to Donje Lapac. There were also some other sporadic incidents in which people who seemed less disciplined, let' say, than those at the fixed checkpoint at Otric denied UN observers certain access to areas. But there was a time, for example, when the Plavno Valley was closed to us. This was a few days after the Grubori incident. There was, in fact, a checkpoint that was established on that single road I mentioned before that went into the Plavno Valley. I'm trying to recall if there was a military or a police checkpoint. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but it was certainly an official checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, generally, who manned these checkpoints, the military, the civilian police, or were they mixed checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: The checkpoint at Otric was a military checkpoint. There were other military checkpoints in Sector South. In the weeks after my arrival, the Croatian police started to set up checkpoints in different locations. So there was somewhat more of a police presence, although I wouldn't say a very widespread police presence.
