utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give a sense of how exactly it operated when, for instance, Mr. Cermak informed you or the other international bodies that restrictions to movement was relaxed and you went out into the field. Was it the case that you could go through those military checkpoints, and prior to that, you would be stopped at these military checkpoints? I'm trying to get it out as to how exactly the restrictions were implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, with respect to Benkovac, for example, well, on my first trip out to Benkovac, we were able to go to Benkovac, and that was on the 13th of August. Before that time, movement was stopped, and I can't speak personally as to how it was stopped. I'm quite sure it was military checkpoints at that point, because this was in the early days following the military offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you personally seen checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who manned those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Croatian military personnel; and after a few weeks, there was some Croatian police checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 2322, please. For the record, that's Human Rights Action Team report 10th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if you want to look at the hard copy, it's at tab 3. Now, there at page 2, the last paragraph, there is a reference to a meeting with Mr. Cermak and General Forand and company. Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Can I review my statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. You have, in fact, referred to it in your 2008 statement at paragraph 8; however, you don't refer to this particular meeting in your statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. I'm not sure if I was present at that meeting; although, on that day, I know that I was at the compound. I wasn't going on a patrol, so I probably was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this document, if you could go back to page 1, in paragraph 4, and I'm referring to the sequence of paragraphs, there is a reference to "safe passage cards." It says "persons at the school ..." Did you note that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus on paragraph 4 on the screen, please. Can you please tell the Court as to how these safe passage cards operated?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, these were documents which allowed individuals to move freely around the area, with the exception, I'm sure, of some areas that might have been blocked off, as I mentioned, with respect to freedom of movement. But in the early days, after Operation Storm, the "propusnica" was the document which, for example, was given to persons inside the compound, Sector South headquarters, which allowed them to move about the area outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you turn to page 4, the attachment, the last paragraph of that document, is that a safe passage card? I think it's not on that tab.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But if you could bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's on the screen, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the "propusnica."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Under whose authorities were these issued?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Under General Cermak's; that's his name on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where were these -- the holders of these cards supposed to produce them at in order to be able to move about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I believe they were to produce them to any military or police authority who stopped them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on. Can you call up document 4065 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if you want to look at hard copies, it's tab 5, Human Rights Action Team report of 12th August 1995. There on page 1, under the subject "Security situation," it refers to a meeting, if you could focus on the paragraph just under "Security situation." It refers to a meeting between Mr. Cermak and General Forand?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of 2008, at paragraph 10, you state that you attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you present throughout that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who else was present?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: The head of political and humanitarian affairs, Mr. Al-Alfi was there; and I say members of HRAT, but actually I'm really not sure who was there. I just know that I was there; and General Forand, of course; General Cermak and colleagues of General Cermak. I'm sure he wasn't alone at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where was it held?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That meeting may have been held at his headquarters. I think it was held at his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, does that report in the Human Rights Action Team report of 12th August, is that an accurate report of what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a reference there to Mr. Cermak being inquired of -- in the next paragraph, it says, "The general responded to an inquiry for information concerning the rash of fires throughout the area by insisting that the phenomenon had no official sanction and that action is being taken by the authorities to stop it." Now, who inquired Mr. Cermak of these rashes of fire in the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm quite sure it was General Forand. In these meetings, it was normally the general who spoke for the United Nations. General Forand was quite concerned about the human rights situation in the area. He was also concerned about the fires, and I know that I had discussed with him this phenomenon of the fires. So I'm virtually certain that General Forand raised the issue with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cermak indicate as to what actions were being taken to stop the fires?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so. I think the response was rather vague, but the general did acknowledge that there was a rash of fires in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to document number 4086, Human Rights Action Team report of 15th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, that's at tab 9 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there in page 1 -- I'm sorry, page 2, the paragraph just -- paragraph numbered 4, under freedom of movement, it is reported that "by order dated 15th August, General Cermak has lifted the necessity for the," I beg your pardon for my pronunciation, "propusnica," safe passage cards, "and directed all checkpoints in Knin to allow the unhindered passage of civilians."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The document on the screen doesn't show -- yes. It's page 2. Next page, please. Page 3 on the -- if you could go down, I'm referring to the paragraph just under freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how did you acquire that information that Mr. Cermak had ordered the lifting the necessity for the safe passage cards?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I think at the UN, at that time, that sort of information would have been communicated very rapidly. I'm not sure if I saw a written order, but an order like that from a general would impact all of our work. So I must have learned from persons involved with the UN, but I can't tell you exactly how I learned of that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But was it implemented? Did you see that decision being implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It was definitely implemented on the ground, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to document number 3084. That is the Human Rights Action Team report of 29th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's at tab 19 [Realtime transcript read in error "tab 9"] of your binder, Mr. Flynn. There in page 1, if you could focus on the last paragraph, it's reported that "General Cermak informed Human Rights Action Team that a report will be provided to them on 30 August regarding the events which occurred in Grubori on 26th August."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "The Croatian authorities have taken the line that the town was a Chetnik stronghold; and that of the dead, unfortunately two were civilians who died in the crossfire. It is claimed that the Croatian authorities have provided humanitarian assistance to citizens remaining in the area." Now, that information, the rest of the paragraph which says the Croatian authorities have taken the position that Grubori was a Chetnik stronghold, so on and so forth, was that conveyed at the meeting when General Cermak informed the Human Rights Action Team that a report would be submitted with regard to the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you present when Mr. Cermak made that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it at a formal meeting, or how -- where was it conveyed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I believe it was in General Cermak's headquarters. General Cermak was fairly open to meeting with us if he was in the area, and meetings didn't always have to be scheduled in advance. So if the Human Rights Action Team requested a meeting with the General, it was sometimes possible to arrange it on very short notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did he indicate at this time, or did you get the sense, that he was stating that the matter was being investigated, the Grubori incident was being investigated at this stage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware, as of this date, on the 30th of -- this report relates 29th August, on 29th August that the Grubori incident was, in fact, being investigated?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm not aware that it was. I was certainly struck about ten days later when I went to Grubori myself and went to the same residence of the dead man whose picture was shown earlier, where there were two bullet casings in the room, and there was still a bullet casing on the floor of that room some ten days to two weeks after the incident. So I personally doubt that a serious investigation took place, at least until that time. Now, maybe in the time afterwards, there was an investigation, I'm not 100 per cent sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you referred to seeing those bullet casings you saw on the 25th of August again ten days after Mr. Cermak made that statement. Was that reported in one of your Human Rights Action Team reports?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 4235 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's at tab 26 of your binder, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's a Human Rights Action Team report for 8th to 11th August [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to the previous document, the transcript, I take it by mistake, refers to "tab 9," where that should be "19." We are now then moving to 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have the document 4235 on the screen, and if you could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, there is a report of the fact that the two bullets -- bullet casings were observed still on the blood-soaked floor of the man's bedroom on this particular patrol which was taken during 8th to 11th August [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: September, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. May I just go back to the document we were looking at earlier on, which is 3084. I beg your pardon for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 19, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 19, yes. There, in that report, if you go to page 2, in the paragraph numbered 5. We're still on the previous document on the screen. Can we go back to document 3084, and page 2 of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a reference there to again a discussion with Mr. Cermak, and there it is reported that "the General stated he is giving an order to that effect to Knin chief of police, Mr. Romanic, that is in reference calling for police reinforcements." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you at this meeting? Was it the same meeting reported in the previous page?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you hear Mr. Cermak say that he would give an order to the Knin chief of police calling for reinforcement? Did you use him use the term "order"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we have document 951 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is tab 21 on your binder, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, it's Human Rights Action Team report of 2nd to 4th September. If you move on to page - I beg your pardon, Mr. President - page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is actually the second paragraph under the subheading "Reports of human rights violations and related issues."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a reference to the observation of burning houses and seeing two uniformed soldiers of the 4th Guards Brigade lounging next to the burning house.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: This is on the first page of the report itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is actually page 2. The first page is a cover page.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the page numbers in the exhibit. That's the second page, but it's the first page. At least it reads page 1 of the Human Rights Action Team Knin daily report, 2nd to the 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note that paragraph which refers to the burning of houses and seeing two soldiers belonging to the 4th Guards Brigade lounging next to the burning houses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote here the "4th Split Brigade." Yeah, I remember that. I was present. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How did you identify the unit the soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: You know, at that time, I may have become familiar with the different markings of soldiers from different units, but I may have also relied on one of my colleagues to help me about that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you described this incident in detail in your 1998 statement, and I'm talking about your first statement, at page 33. If you could go to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need paragraph reference because there is various pagination in various language versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the English version at page 33, line 23 going into page 34, I'm afraid there are no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no paragraphs. It's just an ongoing story, but the lines certainly in the different languages might not correspond. I haven't got a translation in front of me. I always prefer to have at least one translation, also if it's B/C/S, for the Bench, so that we can assist in getting to the right spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could provide one right now, Mr. President, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you first would help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could have a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take often, it's difficult to find numbers or specific capitalis ed text. Is there anything you could find or a specific name? It is close to where the words "Cvijanovici" appears, if that helps the interpreters. It is a paragraph which starts also concerning the incident concerning the Cvijanovici hamlet. It's the first line of the paragraph. I'm just waiting for a signal that the interpreters have found the spot you would like to deal with. In English, it is page 33. Perhaps, Mr. Usher, could get the B/C/S copy for me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have found it in the statement from 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have an indication that the interpreters have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed and provide the usher with a B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at page 33, lines 23 onwards, you refer to this incident of seeing the Croatian soldiers of 4th Split Brigade, as you refer to them, lounging next to the burning structures. And going on to page 34, you state that this incident was reported to someone in General Cermak's office, and I'm referring to page 34, line 4. Who reported that matter to Mr. Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it says, "but I believe," not that it was a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, Mr. Kay points at the text which says, "I'm not sure exactly who we reported it to that day, but I believe that we advised ..." Whereas, in your question, you did put it as a fact, rather than something the witness "believed."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will explore that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, now, you say that you believe that "we advised someone in the office of military headquarters in Knin, someone in General Cermak's office related to that incident." Now, what was the basis for that statement? How did you know or what led you to believe that someone in Mr. Cermak's office was informed of this incident?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I believe I reported it to someone in his office. As I said before, General Cermak's office was fairly available to us, in the sense that we felt that if there was an urgent need, we could go to his office, perhaps meet with the General himself, but if not, meet with one of his colleagues. And after seeing an event or an incident such as we saw in the Plavno Valley, I'm quite sure that we took advantage of that accessibility of General Cermak and his team to report it immediately to them, as we had done a couple of weeks earlier in the case of the Grubori incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I assume that it was a practice on the part of your team to inform Mr. Cermak's office when you observed this type of incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we not have assumption? Can the witness give the evidence, his own evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, what you assume is not to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you clarify the term as to why you say you believed? What was the basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that question has been put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question. You told us that you would go to the office of Mr. Cermak and then either see him or inform people in his office about events. Did it ever appear to you that information which was not directly relayed to Mr. Cermak, that, at a later stage, you experienced that he was unaware of the information you left in his office, although not directly with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It never appeared to me that that was the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call for document 4207, please. That's a Human Rights Action Team report of 7th September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, that's in tab 24 of your binder. On page 1 of that document, paragraph 4, there is a reference to Mr. Cermak saying that what was going on was a shame on Croatia, and he's reported to have said "enough is enough." He has further informed the group of persons he was addressing that the group of persons had been arrested in connection with criminal activity in the sector and the names and locations were unknown. He goes on to say that "HINA," that is referring to a media press, "reported on 6 September that Cermak had a dozen HV soldiers, suspected of having broken the law, have been arrested, and that civilian and military police would set up controls to put up a stop to unlawful acts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's "set up" where it reads "step up." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, from where did you obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: The information regarding General Cermak's reported change of view?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to particularly - initially, I'm referring to Mr. Cermak - when he says that the situation was "a shame on Croatia and that enough was enough."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. That information was reported to me by UN colleagues who met with General Cermak that day, including Mr. Al-Alfi, the head of political and humanitarian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know if that information was discussed or if Mr. Cermak made that statement at a meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi or was it said somewhere else and Mr. Al-Alfi informed you of this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. It was made with a meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi and other UN officials, and Mr. Al-Alfi also included it in a report that he made of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In relation to that, if I may call up document 1581.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is in your tab, Mr. Flynn, at tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, it's a weekly report dated 8th September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the report you just referred to as Mr. Al-Alfi having reported these details of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could move on to page 3 of that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, in paragraph 3, starting with, "During the meeting," it goes on to say, "We raised with General Cermak the question of continuing looting and burning of houses in the area. We further raised specific cases of recent murders which were brought to his attention and asked for the results of the investigation by the Croatian authorities. General Cermak did not deny the continuation of such activities, and said that strict orders have been issued to arrest those who commit such crimes. "He also informed us that they have already one group in custody who will be put before trial. He informed us that, in a recent interview on Croatian television, he dealt with these activities and regarded them as 'a shame on Croatia.' "General Cermak agreed to give his instructions for more joint patrolling between UN CIVPOL and the Croatian police particularly in the remote villages." Is that the report that you have reported in your daily report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this report that is document number 1581, the weekly report, was author the by whom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Al-Alfi's designation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: He was the political and humanitarian affairs coordinator for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take you back to your 1998 statement. In page 22, at lines 17 to 19, you refer to Mr. Cermak making a public statement, essentially expressing his concern about the burning and looting that was taking place at that time. What were you referring to at this stage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Exactly that statement that he made to UN officials in that meeting we just referred to, and to his reference to a media interview that he had given.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on that same page, at lines 22 to 26, you go on to say that "Mr. Cermak expressed his view that there were understandable strong feelings and strong emotions among Croats and Croatian citizens about events that had taken place during the war, including in 1991." You say this was stated by Mr. Cermak on a couple of occasions. Now, do you recall these occasions when Mr. Cermak said this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I know he said that in the interview with UN television that related to the Grubori incident, which I had already seen by the time I gave this statement. He may have said that in meetings with me. I'm just not 100 per cent sure that he did, and I can't remember at this point. But I know he made that statement, as I say, to the UN -- to UN TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to actually his statement about the understandable strong emotions among Croats, and I'm not referring to the statement that he made, where he said that the situation was a shame on Croatia. Do you recall when that was made? Was it made to you at any point of time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It may have been. I just can't recall that specifically. I just can't sit here and say that. As I say, my vivid recollection of that is from this interview that the General gave to UN TV; and in that interview, he referred to the feelings of Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 289, please. That is the Human Rights Action Team report for 12th to 13th September, and that's at tab 27. I believe we are still on the previous document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While the document is being brought up, Mr. Flynn, if I could draw your attention to your 2008 statement, paragraph 35. You refer to the Human Rights Action Team report of 12th to 13th September, which is now on the screen. On page 2, paragraph 2, there is a report on a meeting between Mr. Cermak and members of the UN.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your statement of 2008 at paragraph 35, you say that you were present on 12th September at the meeting with General Cermak when he said that he could not deny that there was serious lawlessness in the sector.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the Human Rights Action Team report, it is reported as this, if I could read it: "In a meeting," --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is at page 2, if we could move on to page 2, and if you could focus on paragraph 2 of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's reported: "In a meeting with the DPHAC and the Centre for Human Rights, on 12th September, military governor General Cermak said he cannot deny that there is serious lawlessness in the sector, and he said he has requested civilian and military police reinforcements from Zagreb who he hopes will arrive by the end of the week. He asked that he be notified immediately if lawlessness is observed, so that he can dispatch police to investigate and arrest the perpetrators if possible." Were you there when he made that entire statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That was in his offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who else was present?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, the DPHAC would be, I believe, Mr. Zhang. He was the deputy coordinator for political and humanitarian affairs. I was the only representative for the Centre of Human Rights at that time. So I have no doubt that I was present and I remember the meeting. I'm not sure exactly who else was there from the UN side or from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what led Mr. Cermak to say that there was no denying that there is serious lawlessness in the sector? What did the participants convey to Mr. Cermak which led to him make that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: We conveyed to the General our continuing concern about lawlessness in the sector. Even in the two or three days prior to that meeting, there had been a number of killings, more burning houses had been observed, there was a high level of looting takes place, and we took that opportunity to report this to General Cermak and his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When Mr. Cermak requested you and the others, it is reported there, that he requested you to inform him if there were any incidents observed, so that he could dispatch police investigators to investigate the crime, did it seem to you that Mr. Cermak, in fact, was just merely saying it to appease you and the international monitors present there, sort of to get away from the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, if ever there was a leading question, I think that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is one. Please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. President. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What were your impressions when Mr. Cermak made that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was a rather remarkable statement to make at that late date. We had notified General Cermak and his office already of a number of incidents of violence and burning and killing, and had requested increased security and police investigations. I think I have to be frank, at the end of that paragraph, I express a certain amount of frustration with the last sentence which you didn't read, and which I add, if I may, Your Honour, a comment, "All the authorities need to do is patrol on their own, and they will find ample persons to investigate and arrest." I thought that was a rather disingenuous assurance for the general to give us at that late stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that comment that is noted there, is that your addition, you noting something, your own impressions in the report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this report and, obviously, this last statement is not, if you will, a report of a factual incident, it's an editorial comment. But I considered it implausible for the general to ask us to notify him of incidents of lawlessness, when, in our travels around the region, it was very easy to see, as I say, burning buildings and acts of looting, and we also investigated at that time a number of killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, it is reported that Mr. Cermak asked -- I'm sorry, that he had requested civilian and military police reinforcements from Zagreb. Now, did he indicate as to from whom he had requested police reinforcement, both civilian police and military police reinforcements? Did he elaborate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't believe so. And speaking for myself, I didn't usually press General Cermak on the question of who he was in contact with in Zagreb. From my point of view, my concern was the local security situation and providing due notice to the General. But I don't recall that we got into the question of who he may have notified in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Taking you back to your statement of 1998. If I could take you to page 9, lines 21 to 28. Lines 21 to 28, you state as follows: "He indicated in his discussions with us, it seemed to me, that he had the authority to tell military units still active in the area what to do or what not to do."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 9. I'm referring to your first statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 9, and if you trace --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- line 21, the portion I'm reading starts from line 22. Referring to General Cermak, you say: "He indicated in his discussions with us, it seemed to me, that he had the authority to tell military units still active in the area what to do or what not to do."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what was it -- what did Mr. Cermak say that led you to believe or conclude that Mr. Cermak had the authority to tell the military units active in the area what to do or what not to do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, General Cermak spoke with great authority about these issues. He didn't say that he would refer matters to others who could take action. We went with him and conveyed concerns, and his response was that he would take the necessary action. He was, indeed, as far as I know, the military governor of the region, and he spoke as if he had the authority to control both military and police and civilian matters in the region. On the other hand, I don't believe that -- or, at that time, I had no impression that General Cermak was, let's say, operationally giving orders to the military, if you will. I mean, he was in Knin, he was dealing with police matters, he was dealing with civilian matters. He was dealing with safe passage, and he was speaking with displaced persons. I think he had a fairly broad area of responsibility. But I can't speak very authoritatively with regard to General Cermak's actual authority. I can only speak with respect to what he indicated to us and seemed to indicate on what I believed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we are on that same page, Mr. Flynn, that is page 9 of your 1998 statement, if you go to line 9, you say that you recall, "Mr. Cermak arrived in Knin a day or two after I did." Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No, that isn't correct. This is a factual error that I noted in this statement long after I gave it; but, apparently, when I gave this statement, I had this recollection. I think this statement is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you -- do you recall when you met Mr. Cermak for the first time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, the first time was on the 8th of August and I had arrived on the 7th of August, but I think there were -- there was also a meeting that took place between UN officials and the general on the 7th. I'm just -- I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you back to document number 2131, which is on tab -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. It's document number 4029, tab 1. That is the Human Rights Action Team report of 8th August. In paragraph 6 on the same page, on page 1 - and when I say paragraph 6, it's the paragraph just under "security situation" - there is a reference, in fact, to a meeting with Mr. Cermak in Knin on 7th August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document number 2403, and that is Human Rights Action Team report for 17th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn it's at tab 12 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then if you could move on to page 2 -- I'm sorry. It should be page 3 because I'm going by the number on the page, the next page. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, there is a reference to an interview with displaced persons at the UN headquarters. It reports on the interview of three persons who arrived at the UN camp, and reported on a killing of four RSK soldiers and civilians travelling in a tractor by members of the HV.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you interview those displaced persons, the refugees who arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to call a document which contains information relating to a protected witness. Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session, and the document should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. It's unnecessary to tell you that, of this one and a half hours, approximately seven and a half minutes are left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm just about to tender my last document which is a map which is outside the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That map is number 65 ter ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be assigned exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P24, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If it can be brought up on the screen, please, and if you could bring up the map on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes some time, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, on Sunday, 6th April, you -- did you examine a map which indicated the locations that you referred to in your reports and your statements?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you satisfied, with the exceptions of a few, a couple of markings, which we will refer to in court now, that the markings properly indicated the locations you referred to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the map contains a legend which names all the locations and gives a number which relates to the markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you a couple of corrections that you needed to make on this map?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Electronically loading maps takes quite a while, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to save time while that's being uploaded, there were a couple of corrections which are not matters of matters in dispute. May I just lead the witness on those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that leading might not be a major problem, but, of course, it depends what kind of corrections you are seeking. But the map is loaded, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the legend at number 8, if you could focus on the legend, at number 8, there is a reference to Rubeje or Rudele. What is the correct name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That would be Rudele.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: R-u-d-e-l-e?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at number 11, on the legend, is the place called Cenici. While Cenici is marked with number 11 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could move down, if we could move down. For the record, Mr. President, Cenici is marked with number 11; however, the location is not marked on the map. And since that has not been indicated on the legend, I wanted to have that place on record. If you could move to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, can you see number 11 there? Number 11 is just below Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could stop there. Yes, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the correct location for Cenici?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But the name is not indicated on this map, simply because this is -- because of the scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the legend at number 15, if we could go back to the legend at number 15. If you could move back, left and up. We should go outside the map area to the legend.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Number 15 and 16, Bakarja and Otocac are mentioned, but those places are not within this map area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, for the record, Mr. President, there is no number 15 and 16 on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it mentioned on the legend.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is on the legend but it is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to look at the legend more precisely. First of all, the first digit disappears, so I can't check what actually is there. You see it starts with 0, 1; but whether that's 10, 11, I've got no idea. May I take it that it starts with 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I think it starts with 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From 1 to 29, I find approximately, well, some 16 or 17; so, therefore, it looks to me as under, if it's 7 -- oh, now we have it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There you are. I'm referring to number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Bakarja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's not found, and although it is in the legend, there is it is not there. And number 16, Otocac, is outside this map area, so there is no marking there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At 21 there is a place referred to as Borovici; however, inadvertently that marking has been left out of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Flynn, mark the location, and if you could take the cursor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The map could be moved to the right, to the extreme right and down. Yes. If you could keep it around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, are you able to indicate where Borovici is, at least the area if you could indicate with your --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. It's north of Knin not too far, but I don't see Knin on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Knin is just below.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. So I think it's a little south of Zelembaba, number 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we at least zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you can see Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a bit from 19, so that we can read what's on the map? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could indicate roughly where Borovici is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it's about -- how to put it. Do you see where it says Grubici? I think it's a little bit south of Grubici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could the witness have a marker, please, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that you want to tender this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if we do the markings on the map, what will remain is the portion of the map zoomed in at, so I take it you want first to tender the map as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then now we need a new exhibit number for that portion of the map, which will be marked by the witness, which will be a separate exhibit, I take it. Because if you store it as it is zoomed in now, you will lose the remainder of the map as an exhibit. So we have done two exhibits: One is the map in its totality marked, although incomplete, by the witness, and then this specific portion of the map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that case, in order to avoid that much of complications, I would just ask the witness to indicate where Borovici is and put it on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perhaps, then, very practical. We have at this moment, in front of us, markings 18 and 19, and a little bit further down is apparently the city of Knin. Could you tell us where we find Borovici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's just a little bit below where you see Grubici, where one can see Grubici there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Grubici is just south of the marking with the number 19. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a little bit south of that, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, if I could give an estimate, approximately the distance from Knin to the place marked number 19, then approximately 80 per cent from Knin, 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my recollection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the legend, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At number 37, there is a reference to, if you could focus on 37, on the legend, there is a reference to Krezevic. Is it Krezevic or is it Knezevic? That is K-n-e-z-e-v-i-c?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It's Knezevic with an N.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, similarly, at 43, there is a reference to Zagorac. Is it Zagorac or Zagrovic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: It's Zagrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's Z-a-g-r-o-v-i-c?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, finally, could you just point out where Kakanj is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could take the map down. And just to assist you, it's below Kistanje, so to the right. Go down and to the right. Yes. If you could stop there and go down further. Yes. If you could stop around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you just point out where Kakanj is? It is just below number 10, Djeverske, a little to the right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness doesn't have to do it any more, because you have done it already, haven't you, Ms. Mahindaratne? It's very practical. I wonder whether this kind of exercise could not have been done outside of court, getting the right spelling where it's apparently doesn't affect. The remaining issue between the parties could have been put to the witness, but this is really -- it's very useful that you're doing it because I always insist on precision. At the same time, there are ways in doing it without spending court time on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I apologise. It's just that this came up with such short notice. We did not time to do it; it was only recent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These are words of encouragement to the parties, to see what minor matters they can settle out of court. But you have indicated and you have given the answer for the witness. That's accepted as it seems. So any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Could the map be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the map tendered into evidence? Then the map is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes the examination in chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll have a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 1.00; and after the break, Mr. Flynn, you will be cross-examined by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the defence counsel to cross-examine the witness, I would first like to give an opportunity to Judge Gwaunza to seek some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, just two short questions. Referring to the video that we saw with those vehicles parked by the side of the road, did you ever get to know, for instance, why those vehicles were there and perhaps what eventually happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I heard, Your Honour, was the reference made in the following days to a special police operation to clean up so-called -- to clean up hold-out RSK fighters who were still in the hills. So I don't recall that the link was made between those vehicles and that operation, but it may have been suggested that they were connected to that activity, because the authorities did suggest to us that there was a military operation against hold-out RSK fighters in the area. But other than that, well that's all the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The other question relates to what you said one of the things you said General Cermak said concerning arrests, arrests made of people who had committed crimes, members of the militia. Did you get to know or confirm that such arrests did actually take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not, Your Honour. I think some other UN colleagues may have, but I personally don't know of any arrests that were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one or two questions. You told us that the explanation given in respect of the Grubori incidents was that it was a stronghold and it was fire fighting, Grubori to be a stronghold, or in this case, strong hold, and keeping out the fighters from that place and then that people might have been caught in crossfire. First of all, that explanation, especially the last portion, crossfire, did that fit into your own observations or the information you obtained on that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I considered it to be implausible in the first place, because the first body we saw was found in a room where bullet casings were evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also the large number of houses which were on fire. I mean, I believe that there might have been some fire caused by a military encounter, but it seemed implausible that all of those fires would have resulted from a military encounter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when this explanation was given to you, did you put to - I think it was Mr. Cermak who gave that explanation - did you put to him that this explanation did not fit into what you observed or what your team had observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I can't recall specifically. We may have, or I may have, referred to those bullets in that room, but I didn't make it a practice to engage in a debate with General Cermak. I always sought his views on relevant matter, but I didn't engage in a debate with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You wouldn't contradict, if you didn't consider it plausible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. What will be the sequence of cross-examination? Mr. Kay, you're on your feet. It seems that you are the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The parties have agreed that I'll go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt for a minute. During the break, there was a discussion between Mr. Gotovina's Defence team and us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed, and the rumours go quickly, usually, is that it has not yet resulted in any agreement. Different versions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We have agreed that the document could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were two issues. The first was whether this statement should be admitted at this moment, and the second is whether there are different versions of that document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. With regard to the second issue, it has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. There's one version, and that's the version we've seen on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the one uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to the first issue, that is document P23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- the interview notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And we do agree that, for the time being, it can be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's usually the first step, and then the Chamber will decide on whether it will be admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because you tendered it. And if you say now that you withdraw tendering it, and ask it to keep the status of marked for identification, then the Chamber will have to consider whether the Chamber accepts that, whether the Chamber calls upon the Prosecution to have that document in evidence and then admitted. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I think the agreement was reached to -- with respect to the Trial Chamber, the agreement was reached to mark it for identification at this moment and not have the Prosecution tender it at this moment, because we wish to continue to discuss trying to resolve it amongst ourselves. There are some other issues in addition to the issues that were raised in front of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I leave it for a while. But the mere fact that once a document is tendered and if it's withdrawn, that the agreement between the parties is not the final word and whether it will be in evidence, yes or no, because the Chamber, of course, has the competence to seek introduction into evidence of a document, especially if it has been used in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we'll leave it then, for the time being, as you agreed, and the Chamber would like to hear from you within three days, by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you by the end of this week. Then Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, you will now be cross-examined by Defence counsel for Mr. Cermak, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, just taking up on the last questions that Judge Orie was asking you, from your evidence, it seems that you were turning to Mr. Cermak for help in relation to the problems that you had in your role of being linked to the UN.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. I wasn't turning to him for help. I was turning to him as the responsible local authority who I believe had responsibility to take action in the event that unlawful activity was determined to be taking place or to have taken place. We turned to General Cermak for help on a number of operational matters, of course, regarding our movement. But our position was that it was the responsibility of the local authorities to conduct investigations into these acts, so I saw my role as one of notifying the local authority about events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your words earlier was you weren't sure of his actual responsibility, and you said that in your evidence earlier today when the issue of the passes were being discussed: "I'm not sure of" General Cermak's "actual authority." I've inserted "General Cermak" there, but you were not sure of his actual authority.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I wouldn't presume to say what arrangements existed within the Croatian military structure with regard to authority for that region. I could only operate on the basis of my own understanding of that structure, and I certainly understood that General Cermak had authority across a range of issues and I approached him on that basis. I was simply stating that I have no inside information with regard to how things operated, once information was transmitted to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the point I'm dealing with, that you were using him to transfer information beyond him, but elsewhere within the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I think I left that to his judgement based on his own responsibility. I operated on the basis that General Cermak himself had authority to obtain certain actions from military authorities, military personnel, police personnel in the region, and I operated on that basis. I'm just saying that I am personally not 100 per cent sure what authority he did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll look at that. But it seems from the terms of your answer, then, that you were making an assumption. You didn't actually know, because you weren't a party to that information.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: That's correct. Someone else within the UN may have been. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So the terms of your evidence, when you discuss his responsibility and give your beliefs, are based upon assumptions that you have made.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, not only assumptions. General Cermak was introduced to me and to my colleagues as the military governor responsible for Sector South. And from the very first encounter I had with him, I based all of my interaction with him on that basis. So it wasn't an assumption drawn out of thin air. It was based on his own presentation of himself and that of other authorities, including local authorities who would say to us, "We can't address that matter. You'll have to talk to General Cermak." That, for example, was a statement that the chief of police made to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just letting the translation move on, on a long answer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at what you said just then, you said that he was introduced to you and to your colleagues as the military governor responsible for Sector South. I just want to examine that because Sector South was a term for a very large region, and it was a region that was identified by the UN.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I would actually like to clarify that, if I may. General Cermak was introduced as the official responsible for an area which roughly coincided with Sector South, but he certainly had no direct link to responsibility for Sector South as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You agree that Sector South, which is the purpose of my question, was a UN designated area and not a Croatian Republic designated area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that geographical assumption appears to have come into your statement about how he was introduced to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next aspect of that sentence, military governor. General Cermak was described to you as being a military governor, not by himself, but by others within the UN.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you actually consider or research or look at what his actual appointment was, what his actual function was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: For my purposes, the important thing to know was that any issues of concern to the UN, generally, could be brought at least to General Cermak. He was the individual that I understood we could go to who had the authority to take action with regard to all matters, including operational matters, freedom of movement, concerns about security, concerns about the continuing presence in the zone of particular military units and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't like interrupting witnesses, and you've given an answer, but I did ask a very specific question. It was whether you'd looked up or researched or considered what his actual authority was and what his position was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I certainly considered it. I did not look it up in the time that I had prior to even knowing that General Cermak had that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll be looking at that later on in my questioning. The first part of your sentence, that he was a person to whom you could address issues of concern and could be brought to his attention, is something I don't agree with. It's the second sentence about his actual authority which you've agreed was based upon a belief of yours.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your role in the Human Rights Action Team arose out of a new concept; is that right? This was not a previously-structured organisation or team prior to August the 4th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: No. A form of it had been implemented in the investigations related to the Srebrenica massacre in July of 1995. In that investigation as well, my office cooperated with other UN entities in investigating events, interviewing witnesses, and that sort of thing. But I would say that, with respect to sort of becoming a formal mechanism that was used to investigate events, it really first came into full play during -- after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'd agree it was a new team?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at a document which arises from the 6th of August, 1995, which you'll probably be familiar with. It's the so-called agreement between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Saranac, the UN and the Croatian government in relation to a post-Operation Storm relationship between the Croatian state and the UN. You're familiar with that document, I presume?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. And, actually, at the time we referred to it fairly regularly, but I don't recall the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at it because it's an important feature of this case, if Your Honours will forgive me from saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to come up on the screen, if I just give a brief description of it which you'll probably agree with, and I'm reading from the head heading, it's an agreement between the government of Croatia, UNCRO on temporary measures in the areas formally known as Sector North and Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will first ask the registrar to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's D28, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of having a clean record, so to speak, so we don't have a big backlog of marked for identifications, this will not be a document in dispute between any of the parties, and so I'd ask that it go into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D28 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, that's a procedure I will try and adopt during my questioning, otherwise we're going to build up a backlog that may be difficult to trace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will notice at the end of this session, Mr. Kay, where you are invited to finish approximately seven minutes before the usual time, that I'll try to get rid of a lot of MFIs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I'm looking for it on a screen. I don't know if anyone else has it. I don't have it on the monitor here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you got it, Mr. Flynn, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good. Should we just look at it. It's a document that's concerned with civilians being involved in hostilities, their humanitarian needs, and their human rights and humanitarian law. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, forgive me for interrupting, but I've lost the picture from my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite honest, I see on my screen no computer evidence, so, therefore -- now we have it. At least I have it and I see are my colleagues also have it on their screens. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will see that I'm reading from the preamble to the numerated paragraphs of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just go through this quickly, Mr. Flynn, you can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, one tiny little thing. The text speaks about civilian population affected by the hostilities, but as you said "involved," which might be different. But I see the document now for the first time. "Involved," in my understanding of the English language, is that you take a role here in being affected by it, and that you are not activity involved. I don't know whether that's a wrong understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was using the word in a slightly different way. I "caught up in."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever I have a problem with the language, I will put it to you, so in order to verify whether I do understand a language which is not my native language correctly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see in paragraph 1 that Croatia expressed its complete and unequivocal commitment to full respect of human rights. These issues that we're looking at were reasons why HRAT became involved in this particular phase of events, is that right, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm not sure there was a direct link, because there was an agreement between the government of Croatia and UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I think we would have continued. We had an independent mandate as human rights officers, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. At paragraph 2, "Croatia concurs that UNCRO, together with UNHCR and ICRC, where appropriate, will monitor and report on human rights situations in the areas and intervene with the Croatian authorities on human rights matters when appropriate." That's right, that was part of the mandate, and would that would that have been part of the agreement that you were working under?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Although, it doesn't specify HRAT there, this can be applied to the terms of your role in the region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, "Croatia encourages all those previous inhabitants who wish to remain peacefully in the areas over which Croatian authority is exercised. However, Croatia will allow, with full guarantees for security, the departure from those areas of all those who express their desire to do so, except those who committed violations of international criminal law." And, in fact, that was a procedure that was part of your concern, or came across your desk, if I can put it that way, rather than using "concern" in one of a number of ways. But it was something that you were involved in and were aware of about the desire that some people may have to leave the region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But there was an exception to that, "except those who committed violations of international criminal law."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, that issue of those who had committed war crimes, in effect, who had been living within the Republika Srpska Krajina was a matter that the UN had recognised Croatia had a legitimate interest to deal with?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Croatia was under an obligation to help UNCRO and other organisations to enable departures in a civili sed way?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm just reaching the end of my screen here, if someone could scroll down, please. Can I scroll down? I'm not sure if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know. This is out of my control.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Can I manipulate this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid you cannot manipulate it; but if you ask to scroll it in a way, then it will be done for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It's being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Just let me read that last sentence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm referring to this document because it forms, in fact, part of the background of your job and what you were looking at, and what was discussed between the UN and General Cermak were elements concerning this agreement between the UN and the government of Croatia. That's right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, if we can move on the English version, "Full access by UNCRO and humanitarian organisations to the civilian population for providing humanitarian needs, but subject to the extent allowed by objective security consideration." That's right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, that formed part of the background concerning the issues of your freedom of movement and restriction of movement was this issue about security considerations? That's right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Whether that was relevant to our work?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I think this paragraph refers more to the provision of humanitarian needs of the population, but equally our movement was subject to objective security considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 5, "UNMO's and human rights monitoring elements," and within that phrase, we would include you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Will carry out surveillance immediately in all areas, except where, in the opinion of the local UNCRO military commanders after consulting Croatian army commanders, the security situation does not permit for such surveillance."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, this issue of security which is relevant to those issues raised during your evidence concerning restriction of movement and freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: I can accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Just for the record, you and I know you agree, but if you could use the word "yes."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Flynn. Looking at paragraph 6, "Croatia will ensure that civilian areas are not targeted." Paragraph 7, "if UNCRO commanders are aware of a particular movement of local military personnel, information will be immediately passed to the Croatian army."
